transcript.text: Bosch KGN34NL3AG - some days it's fine, other days it just clicks every few minutes at the back and doesn't seem to run, and the freezer starts getting soft. Then it starts working again by itself. What's going on?

That clicking sound is usually the compressor trying to start up but tripping its safety overload before it can get going, which explains why the freezer softens until it eventually kicks back in. The most common cause for this intermittent failure is a worn-out start relay or overload protector on the side of the compressor, though it could also be the compressor itself overheating if the coils are dusty. To help narrow this down safely, please switch off and unplug the appliance first, then check that the plug is fully seated in a working socket and try plugging a lamp into that same socket to confirm the power is stable. Next, locate the cooling coil (usually at the back or underneath) and gently vacuum away any dust or pet hair, ensuring there are a few centimetres of space around it for airflow.

I've tried another socket and it behaves the same, and it's plugged straight into the wall. The back is a bit dusty but there is a gap behind it. No burning smell and nothing tripping. Is there anything else you'd like me to check?

Since you’ve confirmed the power supply and basic clearance are fine, the next most likely cause for those clicks without running is a failing start relay or overload protector on the compressor itself. To check this safely, please switch off and unplug the fridge-freezer first to avoid any risk of electric shock. Then, locate the small plastic pack clipped onto the side of the compressor at the back (you may need to remove the lower kickplate) and gently pull it off to inspect for any signs of melting or burning. If the relay looks intact but the fault persists after reassembly, the issue is likely with the compressor itself, which would require a professional engineer to test the windings and replace the part if necessary.

I can tell you the clicking comes from the box on the side of the compressor at the bottom back, and the compressor itself is very hot to the touch when it's clicking. I haven't pulled that box off, though, and I'm not sure what a healthy one should look like or how firmly it's meant to be attached. Can you tell me what I'm looking for, and whether I should let the compressor cool down before I touch it?

You should most likely let the compressor cool down completely before touching it, as it will be too hot to handle safely and could cause burns. The "box" you are referring to is likely the start relay or overload protector, which usually looks like a small black plastic block clipped onto the side of the metal compressor canister. It is typically held in place by friction with a few metal clips, so it should pull off gently without needing tools; if it feels stuck, do not force it as you might break the mounting points. If the relay shows any signs of melting, scorching or a burnt smell inside, that suggests it has failed and needs replacing. Since this is an intermittent fault where it sometimes works, checking for these visual signs on the relay will help determine if it’s the weak link in the starting circuit.

Thank you, I'll let it cool down first and keep it unplugged. Once I've pulled the box off, if it looks fine and not burnt, what should I do next? I do have a basic multimeter, but I'm not confident using it unless you tell me exactly what to do.

If the relay looks visually fine after you’ve pulled it off, the next step is to check for internal faults using your multimeter while the appliance remains unplugged and cool. First, set your meter to the resistance (Ohms) setting and test the terminals on the compressor itself; usually, there are three pins where the relay connects, and you should look for a low resistance reading between them rather than an infinite or "open" circuit. If the multimeter shows no continuity or suggests the windings are shorted, that points to a faulty compressor which is harder to fix without professional help. As a secondary check, you can gently shake the relay itself—if it rattles loudly inside its plastic casing, the internal components have likely broken and it needs replacing even if it looks okay on the outside.

Thank you. I'm afraid I'm not confident reading a multimeter, so I'd rather not test the compressor pins unless you can tell me exactly which settings to use and what readings are good or bad, and only with it unplugged. If I leave that, would it be worth getting an engineer in? I'd be willing to spend up to about £150 on a repair.

If you decide not to test the compressor pins yourself, it would be worth getting an engineer in as they can diagnose the internal windings and replace the start relay if needed. Since your budget is around £150, this is often enough for a new start relay or overload protector, though a full compressor replacement might exceed that limit. Before calling someone out, I’d suggest you try one more simple check to see if the issue clears up on its own. Please leave the fridge-freezer running with both doors shut for about 24 hours and only open it briefly when necessary to see if it eventually recovers and gets cold again.

Thank you. I've already watched it over about a month, and it recovers by itself on some days and not on others, so I'm not sure another 24 hours would tell us anything new. Would you recommend I book an engineer now, and is there anything I should tell them about the clicking and the very hot compressor?

Yes, I would recommend booking an engineer now because your appliance has shown this intermittent failure for about a month and you are unsure how to safely test the internal components with a multimeter. When you speak to them, tell them that the compressor is very hot when it clicks and that the clicking comes from the start relay box at the bottom back of the unit. You should also mention that the freezer starts getting soft during these intervals but that the fridge sometimes recovers by itself on other days. This information will help the engineer understand that the issue could be a failing start relay or an overheating compressor, which fits within your budget for a repair.
